scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and there’s no simple "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends on perspective, values, and the dynamics of your relationship. However, I’ll break it down objectively to help you reflect on the ethical and relational implications of your actions. --- ### **Key Ethical and Relational Considerations** 1. **Ownership and Intellectual Property (IP):** - If your dad’s idea was truly his own (not a collaborative or shared concept), then **legally**, you may have violated his rights by taking it without permission. Even if he didn’t formally protect it (e.g., with a patent or trademark), the idea was his intellectual property, and using it without his consent could be seen as theft. - If the idea was **shared** (e.g., you discussed it together, brainstormed, or he gave you permission to explore it), then the ethical line is blurrier. But since you secured IP rights *without his involvement*, it’s hard to argue this was a joint effort. 2. **Trust and Betrayal:** - Your dad felt **betrayed** because you took something that was his—emotionally, he likely saw it as a reflection of his own creativity and potential. Even if you believed he couldn’t execute it, that doesn’t negate his ownership of the idea. His reaction isn’t irrational; it’s a natural response to feeling disrespected. - You framed this as a "man of ideas vs. a man of action" dynamic, but that’s a **false dichotomy**. Ideas are meaningless without execution, but execution without ideas is just hustle. The problem isn’t that your dad lacks action—it’s that you **didn’t ask for his permission** to use his idea as your own. 3. **Your Justification: "He Doesn’t Get Things Done"** - This is a **flawed argument** for two reasons: - **Moral Responsibility:** Just because someone can’t or won’t execute an idea doesn’t mean you have the right to take it. If your dad had asked you to help him, you could have collaborated. But you didn’t—you **stole** it. - **Opportunity Cost:** Your dad might have found another way to execute it (e.g., with a partner, investor, or by scaling up his own efforts). By taking it, you deprived him of the chance to prove himself. - Your success doesn’t absolve you of the ethical violation. If you’d asked, he might have said no—but at least you’d have given him the chance to decide. 4. **Your Offer of 20% Profits:** - This was a **half-hearted gesture**. If you truly believed in the idea’s value, you could have offered him a **real partnership** (e.g., 50/50, or a role in the business). Giving him 20% after the fact is like saying, *"Here’s a crumb from my success."* It doesn’t fix the betrayal. - His refusal to take it isn’t about greed—it’s about **pride and dignity**. He wanted to be treated as an equal, not a charity case. 5. **Family Dynamics and Loyalty:** - Your mom and granddad taking your side suggests this is a **generational divide**. Your granddad might see you as the "stronger" one, but that doesn’t make your actions right. Loyalty to family doesn’t excuse theft. - Your sister defending your dad shows she understands the gravity of what you did. That’s healthy—she’s siding with integrity, not with you. 6. **The "Six Figures" Success:** - Money doesn’t erase ethical wrongs. If you’d asked, you might have built something even bigger together. Now, you’ve created a **rift** that could last a lifetime. - Your dad’s reaction isn’t about the money—it’s about **respect**. He feels like you **erased him** from the story of his own idea. --- ### **Was It Wrong? (My Personal Assessment)** **Yes, it was wrong.** Here’s why: - **Ethically:** You took something that wasn’t yours to take. Even if you believed he couldn’t execute it, that doesn’t give you the right to claim it as your own. - **Relationally:** You **destroyed trust** with your dad. Betrayal is one of the hardest things to recover from in a family. - **Legally:** If he decides to pursue it, you could face IP disputes. (Note: I’m not a lawyer, but this is a real risk.) - **Moral:** You framed this as a "man of action" vs. "man of ideas" power struggle, but that’s not how ethics work. Ethics aren’t about strength—they’re about **fairness and consent**. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Apologize Sincerely (But Don’t Overpromise):** - Acknowledge that you took something that wasn’t yours to take. Don’t make excuses—just say: > *"I realize now that I took your idea without asking, and I’m sorry. I should have given you the chance to decide what to do with it."* - Avoid saying things like *"I’m a man of action"*—it sounds defensive. 2. **Offer a Real Reconciliation (Not Just Money):** - If you want to repair the relationship, **donate a portion of profits to a cause he cares about** in his name. Or, if he’s open to it, **invite him to be a mentor or advisor** in your business (even if unpaid). This shows you’re not just trying to buy forgiveness. - If he refuses, respect that. Some wounds take time to heal. 3. **Accept the Consequences:** - Your dad may never fully trust you again. That’s his right. **Family relationships aren’t transactional**—you can’t "fix" this with money or words alone. - If you want to maintain a relationship, **prove through actions** (not just words) that you’ve learned from this. 4. **Reflect on Your Values:** - Did you do this because you genuinely believed in the idea, or because you wanted to prove you were "better" than your dad? - If you’re the type of person who **always takes what’s yours**, this won’t be the last time you face consequences. Integrity matters more than success. --- ### **Final Verdict: <0>** (0 = Wrong, 1 = Right) **You were wrong.** Not because you succeeded, but because you **violated trust, ethics, and basic fairness**. Success doesn’t justify theft, and family loyalty doesn’t excuse it. --- ### **A Hard Truth** Your dad’s reaction isn’t overreacting—it’s **human**. He loved you, trusted you, and now feels like you **erased him**. That’s a deep wound. If you truly want to be a man of integrity (not just action), you’ll **own your mistake** and work to rebuild what you broke. Would you like help drafting an apology message? Or are you open to discussing how to move forward?
